elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to an Affiliate without consent.
elements.evidence: Section 15.6 permits PB to assign the Agreement and all rights and obligations to any Affiliate, notwithstanding the general consent requirement.

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement without consent to a successor in a merger.
elements.evidence: PB may assign to a successor in connection with a transfer of all or substantially all relevant business or assets, expressly including a merger.

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement without consent to a successor in an acquisition.
elements.evidence: The successor exception covers a sale or other transfer, including a sale of stock or otherwise, which encompasses an acquisition.

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement without consent to a successor in a sale of substantially all assets.
elements.evidence: The clause expressly permits PB to assign to a successor in connection with a transfer of all or substantially all of the business or assets to which the Agreement relates.

elements.element: Vendor may assign the Agreement only with Customer's prior written consent.
elements.evidence: The general prohibition requires the other Party's prior written consent, and the Affiliate/successor exception is limited to PB, so SFJ has no consent-free assignment exception.

elements.element: For any Vendor assignment that is not to a Customer competitor, Customer's consent may not be unreasonably withheld.
elements.evidence: Although the opening language says consent for an SFJ assignment will not be unreasonably withheld, the notwithstanding sentence absolutely prohibits transfers to every entity whose primary business is pharmaceutical or biotechnology development or commercialization. Because that category is not limited to PB competitors, some non-competitor assignments are excluded from the reasonable-consent regime.

elements.element: Vendor may never assign the Agreement to a Customer competitor.
elements.evidence: The permanent prohibition is based on the transferee's primary business, not whether the transferee competes with PB. It may capture non-competitors and may omit a PB competitor whose primary business falls outside the stated category.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate the Agreement because of Customer's change of control.
elements.evidence: Section 14.2.6 expressly states that SFJ has no right to terminate the Agreement as a result of a Change of Control of PB.

elements.element: Customer may assign the Agreement to a successor without consent.
elements.evidence: PB has a consent-free right to assign to a successor in connection with the specified merger, stock sale, asset sale, or other transfer.

elements.element: Vendor may assign the Agreement to a successor without consent.
elements.evidence: The successor exception is limited to PB. SFJ remains subject to PB's prior written consent and, for the stated pharmaceutical/biotechnology transferee category, an absolute prohibition.

elements.element: Customer must provide written notice when assigning the Agreement to a successor.
elements.evidence: Section 15.6 imposes no notice requirement for PB's successor assignment. The separate PB Change of Control notice does not cover every successor assignment, including all qualifying asset transfers.

elements.element: Vendor must provide written notice when assigning the Agreement to a successor.
elements.evidence: No written-notice mechanism is provided for an SFJ successor assignment; instead, SFJ must obtain PB's prior written consent.

elements.element: Customer assignments other than successor assignments require Vendor's consent.
elements.evidence: PB may assign to any Affiliate without SFJ's consent, even though an Affiliate assignment need not be a successor assignment.

elements.element: Vendor assignments other than successor assignments require Customer's consent.
elements.evidence: SFJ has no Affiliate, successor, or other consent-free exception, so its assignments remain subject to PB's prior written consent, with the stated transferee category prohibited altogether.

elements.element: Vendor may not unreasonably withhold consent to Customer assignments other than successor assignments.
elements.evidence: The reasonableness qualifier applies only to consent for an assignment by SFJ. SFJ's consent to an assignment by PB is not restricted by a reasonableness standard.

elements.element: Customer may not unreasonably withhold consent to Vendor assignments other than successor assignments.
elements.evidence: The clause states this standard generally for SFJ assignments, but the notwithstanding sentence categorically prohibits a class of SFJ transfers regardless of whether withholding consent would be reasonable. The fallback requires the reasonable-consent regime for all non-successor assignments.

result.reason: Treating PB as Customer and SFJ as Vendor, the redline substantially implements the preferred structure but does not use a competition-based prohibition. Its industry-based absolute ban is both potentially overinclusive and underinclusive, and it also prevents some non-competitor assignments from receiving the promised reasonable-consent treatment. The fallback fails because successor rights and notice are not mutual, PB retains a consent-free Affiliate exception, and the reasonableness standard is not mutual. The changes generally preserve unrelated terms, but they are not minimal because the industry-wide transfer prohibition goes beyond the requested competitor restriction. Drafting quality is also reduced by the dangling 'and' before the notwithstanding paragraph and the mismatch between the margin comment's competitor concept and the operative language.
